recommended_actions.intro: This plan helps the community prepare for the heat.

items.text: Keep the home cooler by covering windows with curtains or shades, and find nearby cool public places you can go to during the hottest days.
Keep drinking water within easy reach of everyone at home so people can drink regularly on hot days.
Note the older people, young children, pregnant women and people with chronic illness nearby whom you will check on during hot days.
Learn the signs of heat illness, such as heavy sweating, dizziness, confusion, fainting or hot dry skin, and know how to contact local emergency services or the nearest health facility.
Follow weather forecasts and any official heat warnings issued by local authorities.
Take aspirin if you feel hot.
Drink water regularly through the day.
Avoid heavy activity during the hottest part of the day and rest in the coolest place available.
If you need to go outside, stay in the shade and wear a wide hat and loose, light-coloured clothing.
Take cool showers or baths and cook less with the oven; do not rely on a fan as your main way to cool down.
Check regularly on older family members, neighbours and young children, and never leave children or pets in a parked vehicle.
If someone is confused, faints or has very hot, dry skin, contact local emergency services or the nearest health facility immediately, move them to a cool shaded place and cool them with wet cloths.
Keep drinking water regularly while it stays hot, and refill stored drinking water for the next hot spell.
Rest and recover in a cool place; if cramps or tiredness from the heat appear, move somewhere cooler, remove extra clothing and sip water.
If heat cramps or exhaustion get worse or last more than an hour, contact a health provider or the nearest health facility.
Keep checking on vulnerable neighbours and relatives until the heat has passed.
Plan heavy outdoor work around the forecast, moving it away from the midday heat where possible.
Arrange shaded rest areas close to the work site before hot days.
Make sure enough drinking water is available at the work site.
Learn the early signs of heat stress and agree in advance how the team will contact local emergency services or the nearest health facility from the work site.
Drink water regularly throughout the work shift.
Take regular rest breaks in the shade or another cool place.
Work in the shade where possible and wear a wide hat and loose, light-coloured clothing.
Avoid high-energy tasks during midday heat if possible.
Watch co-workers for signs of heat stress, especially older workers, pregnant workers and people with chronic health conditions.

Heat exhaustion and heat stroke need an emergency response: if a worker is confused, faints or collapses, stop work, move them to shade, cool them and contact local emergency services or the nearest health facility.
After the shift, rest in a cool place, remove extra clothing and sip water to recover.
If cramps or exhaustion after work get worse or last more than an hour, contact a health provider or the nearest health facility.
Check the forecast for the coming days and adjust work schedules to it.
Before hot spells, mulch to keep soil moist and plan shade for vegetable crops.
Store extra water for people, animals and crops before the heat arrives.
Prepare shade for animals kept outside and make sure barns and sheds are well ventilated.
Follow local weather forecasts and crop advisories so you can plan ahead.
Know how to contact local emergency services or the nearest health facility, and keep the contact of a local veterinarian or extension worker for sick animals.
Give animals a continuous supply of cool, clean water, and drink water regularly yourself.
Do field work and handle animals in the early morning or evening, and feed cattle in cooler hours.
Take rest and water breaks in the shade during field work.
Keep animals that are outside in the shade, and give priority to shade for poultry, which cannot sweat.
Irrigate in the cooler hours of the day and keep harvested produce out of the sun.

If a person is confused, faints or has hot, dry skin, contact local emergency services or the nearest health facility; if animals look lethargic or have dry or sunken eyes, contact a local veterinarian.
After the heat, watch livestock for breathing and digestive problems.
Keep animal water clean and fresh, since warm stagnant water can grow toxic blue-green algae.
Rest in a cool place after field work and sip water to recover.
Contact a local veterinarian or extension worker about animals that are still unwell after the heat.

checklist_markdown:
# Heatwave preparedness checklist

**Not verified - needs human review.** Only items that passed automated safety checks are listed.

_The plan did not pass automated safety verification after one revision. A person should review it before it is shared._

## Households

### Before the heat
- [ ] Keep the home cooler by covering windows with curtains or shades, and find nearby cool public places you can go to during the hottest days.
- [ ] Keep drinking water within easy reach of everyone at home so people can drink regularly on hot days.
- [ ] Note the older people, young children, pregnant women and people with chronic illness nearby whom you will check on during hot days.
- [ ] Learn the signs of heat illness, such as heavy sweating, dizziness, confusion, fainting or hot dry skin, and know how to contact local emergency services or the nearest health facility.
- [ ] Follow weather forecasts and any official heat warnings issued by local authorities.

### During the heat
- [ ] Drink water regularly through the day.
- [ ] Avoid heavy activity during the hottest part of the day and rest in the coolest place available.
- [ ] If you need to go outside, stay in the shade and wear a wide hat and loose, light-coloured clothing.
- [ ] Take cool showers or baths and cook less with the oven; do not rely on a fan as your main way to cool down.
- [ ] Check regularly on older family members, neighbours and young children, and never leave children or pets in a parked vehicle.
- [ ] If someone is confused, faints or has very hot, dry skin, contact local emergency services or the nearest health facility immediately, move them to a cool shaded place and cool them with wet cloths.

### After the heat
- [ ] Keep drinking water regularly while it stays hot, and refill stored drinking water for the next hot spell.
- [ ] Rest and recover in a cool place; if cramps or tiredness from the heat appear, move somewhere cooler, remove extra clothing and sip water.
- [ ] If heat cramps or exhaustion get worse or last more than an hour, contact a health provider or the nearest health facility.
- [ ] Keep checking on vulnerable neighbours and relatives until the heat has passed.

## Outdoor workers

### Before the heat
- [ ] Plan heavy outdoor work around the forecast, moving it away from the midday heat where possible.
- [ ] Arrange shaded rest areas close to the work site before hot days.
- [ ] Make sure enough drinking water is available at the work site.
- [ ] Learn the early signs of heat stress and agree in advance how the team will contact local emergency services or the nearest health facility from the work site.

### During the heat
- [ ] Drink water regularly throughout the work shift.
- [ ] Take regular rest breaks in the shade or another cool place.
- [ ] Work in the shade where possible and wear a wide hat and loose, light-coloured clothing.
- [ ] Avoid high-energy tasks during midday heat if possible.
- [ ] Watch co-workers for signs of heat stress, especially older workers, pregnant workers and people with chronic health conditions.
- [ ] Heat exhaustion and heat stroke need an emergency response: if a worker is confused, faints or collapses, stop work, move them to shade, cool them and contact local emergency services or the nearest health facility.

### After the heat
- [ ] After the shift, rest in a cool place, remove extra clothing and sip water to recover.
- [ ] If cramps or exhaustion after work get worse or last more than an hour, contact a health provider or the nearest health facility.
- [ ] Check the forecast for the coming days and adjust work schedules to it.

## Farmers

### Before the heat
- [ ] Before hot spells, mulch to keep soil moist and plan shade for vegetable crops.
- [ ] Store extra water for people, animals and crops before the heat arrives.
- [ ] Prepare shade for animals kept outside and make sure barns and sheds are well ventilated.
- [ ] Follow local weather forecasts and crop advisories so you can plan ahead.
- [ ] Know how to contact local emergency services or the nearest health facility, and keep the contact of a local veterinarian or extension worker for sick animals.

### During the heat
- [ ] Give animals a continuous supply of cool, clean water, and drink water regularly yourself.
- [ ] Do field work and handle animals in the early morning or evening, and feed cattle in cooler hours.
- [ ] Take rest and water breaks in the shade during field work.
- [ ] Keep animals that are outside in the shade, and give priority to shade for poultry, which cannot sweat.
- [ ] Irrigate in the cooler hours of the day and keep harvested produce out of the sun.
- [ ] If a person is confused, faints or has hot, dry skin, contact local emergency services or the nearest health facility; if animals look lethargic or have dry or sunken eyes, contact a local veterinarian.

### After the heat
- [ ] After the heat, watch livestock for breathing and digestive problems.
- [ ] Keep animal water clean and fresh, since warm stagnant water can grow toxic blue-green algae.
- [ ] Rest in a cool place after field work and sip water to recover.
- [ ] Contact a local veterinarian or extension worker about animals that are still unwell after the heat.
